explanation: Vertical scaling is simple because the architecture does not change, but the biggest available machine is a hard ceiling and the machine is still a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling removes that ceiling at the cost of distribution problems such as state sharing and consistency.
options: It requires rewriting the application for every upgrade.
It has a hard ceiling: a single machine can only get so big, and it remains a single point of failure.
It cannot improve latency for a single user.
It forces all data to be sharded across machines.
prompt: What is the main limitation of vertical scaling compared with horizontal scaling?
title: Vertical vs horizontal scaling

explanation: CAP says that during a partition a system can guarantee at most two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. Since partitions happen in real networks, the practical choice is consistency versus availability while partitioned: refuse some requests to stay consistent, or answer with possibly stale data to stay available.
options: It must sacrifice partition tolerance and shut down entirely.
It must sacrifice either consistency or availability, but not both.
It must sacrifice durability, losing all recent writes.
It must sacrifice latency, but can keep consistency and availability.
prompt: A distributed store is partitioned: two groups of replicas cannot communicate. According to the CAP theorem, what must it sacrifice?
title: CAP theorem during a partition

explanation: Write-through writes to cache and database together, so the cache cannot serve a value older than the latest write, but each write pays the cost of both stores. Cache-aside can serve stale data between a write and its invalidation, write-behind risks loss if the cache crashes before flushing, and TTL is an expiry mechanism, not a write pattern.
options: Cache-aside, because the application populates the cache on a miss.
Write-through, because every write goes to the cache and the database together.
Write-behind, because writes are flushed to the database asynchronously.
TTL expiry, because entries disappear after a fixed time.
prompt: Which caching pattern guarantees the cache is never stale after a write, at the cost of slower writes?
title: Write-through caching

explanation: At-least-once delivery can redeliver a message after a crash or timeout, so a consumer that is not idempotent would apply the same order or payment twice. Acknowledging before processing would lose messages on crash, global ordering is a separate and expensive property, and in-memory-only storage loses messages on broker restart.
options: Acknowledge each message before processing it.
Be idempotent, so processing a redelivered message twice has the same effect as once.
Process messages strictly in global order.
Store messages in memory only, for speed.
prompt: A queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. What must its consumers do?
title: At-least-once delivery

back: Many requests miss at once when a popular key expires, and all hammer the database. Mitigate by letting one request repopulate the cache while others wait or serve the stale value, staggering TTLs with jitter, or warming the cache before expiry.
front: What is a thundering herd in caching, and how do you mitigate it?
title: Thundering herd

back: Push (fan-out on write) optimises reads with precomputed feeds but is expensive for celebrity posters. Pull (fan-out on read) makes writes cheap but reads expensive when a user follows many accounts. The standard answer is a hybrid: push for ordinary users, a pull path for celebrities.
front: Push vs pull fan-out for a news feed: what does each optimise, and what breaks each?
title: Push vs pull fan-out

back: Single Responsibility: one class, one reason to change. Open/Closed: extend without modifying. Liskov Substitution: subclasses usable wherever the parent is expected. Interface Segregation: small focused interfaces, not one fat one. Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concretions.
front: State each SOLID principle in one line.
title: SOLID in one line each

explanation: Base62 uses digits 0-9, lowercase a-z, then uppercase A-Z, so digit values 0-61 map to '0'-'9', 'a'-'z', 'A'-'Z'. 125 = 2 x 62 + 1, giving digits 2 and 1, printed most-significant first as "21". The value 0 is a special case returning "0".
options: "21" then ""
"2B" then "0"
title: Base62 encoding output

explanation: The bucket starts with 10 tokens (capacity) and no measurable time passes during the instant loop, so almost no refill occurs. The first 10 requests consume the 10 tokens and the remaining 3 are rejected, giving 10 accepted. This is the burst allowance of a token bucket: up to capacity instantly, then only as fast as the refill rate.
prompt: A TokenBucket is created with refill 10 per second and capacity 10, starting full. Three requests arrive instantly, then 10 more arrive instantly. How many of the 13 requests are accepted?
title: Token bucket behaviour

description: Implement Base62.encode(long value): return the base62 representation using alphabet "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ", most-significant digit first. Encode 0 as "0". Assume value is non-negative.
hints: Repeatedly take value % 62 for the next digit and divide value by 62.
Digits are produced least-significant first, so reverse at the end.
title: Base62 encode

description: Implement a thread-safe TokenBucket with a constructor taking refillPerSecond and capacity, starting full, and a tryAcquire() method returning true and consuming one token when a token is available, false otherwise. Refill tokens continuously at refillPerSecond, capped at capacity.
examples: new TokenBucket(10, 10), 10 immediate tryAcquire() calls → all true, 11th → false
new TokenBucket(1, 1), tryAcquire() → true, then immediate tryAcquire() → false
hints: Track lastRefillNanos and add elapsed seconds times refillPerSecond on each call.
Cap tokens at capacity and synchronise tryAcquire so concurrent callers cannot overspend.
title: Token bucket rate limiter

description: Implement ExpenseSplitter.addExpense(paidBy, amount, participants) and balanceOf(user): the payer's balance increases by the full amount, each participant's balance decreases by amount divided by the number of participants (the payer is included in participants when they share the cost). A positive balance means the user is owed money; an unknown user has balance 0.
hints: Use Map.merge with Double::sum so first and repeat entries are handled uniformly.
Apply the payer credit first, then subtract the share from every participant.
title: Equal expense split

description: Design a URL shortener serving 100 million new URLs per month with far more redirects than creations. State your requirements, capacity estimate, short-code strategy, and how you keep redirects fast and analytics from slowing them down.
solution: Clarify: shorten, redirect, optional custom aliases, click counts; out of scope is link expiry unless asked. Estimate: 100M/month is about 40 creations per second on average, and redirects dominate reads, so this is read-heavy. Generate codes either by hashing the long URL (handling collisions) or by encoding a counter id in base62 (guaranteeing uniqueness, needing an available counter service). Keep redirects fast with a cache of short code to long URL in front of a replicated database, since most redirects hit popular links. Keep analytics off the redirect path: enqueue click events and aggregate them asynchronously, so analytics can never slow down or fail a redirect. Name the bottleneck: the counter service or the primary database on writes, and the cache on hot keys.
title: Design a URL shortener

description: Design a parking lot with motorcycle, car, and bus spots, tickets on entry, and payment on exit. State your classes, how spots are claimed concurrently, and how pricing can change without editing parking logic.
solution: Classes: Vehicle (plate, type), ParkingSpot (number, allowed type, parked vehicle), ParkingLot (spot pools per type), Ticket (vehicle, spot, entry time, pricing), and a PricingStrategy interface. Claim a spot atomically: synchronise the check-and-park step so two threads cannot claim the same free spot. On exit, the ticket computes the fee through its PricingStrategy and the spot is freed. Pricing changes by adding a new PricingStrategy implementation (hourly, daily, surge) without touching Vehicle, Spot, or Lot code. Edge cases: full lot (reject with a clear message), wrong vehicle type for a spot, and a ticket presented twice.
title: Design a parking lot
